replying_to: Replying to Model Editing as a Robust and Denoised variant of DPO: A Case Study on Toxicity
display_title: Official Review of Submission13296 by Reviewer 2Wyh

summary.value: In this paper, the authors propose to align large language models by projecting out subspaces from late-layer MLPs in the LLM. This is then shown to be connected to DPO in one layer. Good performance is seen across a range of models for toxicity, and some initial results are obtained for broader-spectrum alignment.

strengths.value:
This approach successfully matches or even outperforms DPO, with a fraction of the training cost. If it fully generalizes to broad-spectrum alignment goals, this could be a powerful approach for cheaply aligning open source models. 

The presentation is thorough and well-written, and the authors have provided extensive numerical experiments despite having limited GPU hardware.

weaknesses.value:
While the experimental results are quite extensive and thorough, only DPO is compared against (and only with the default hyperparameters). See "Questions" below for a possible suggestion to expand comparisons by referring to benchmark experiments in the literature.

Experimental results could be made more readable by more prominently defining metrics, and indicating whether higher or lower is better. 

Minor style point: Throughout, "inter alia" is used, but I believe "etc." is probably the more preferred Latin phrase here.

questions.value:
As far as I can tell, the proposed method is only compared against DPO, while other methods like KTO, IPO, and AOT exist and can outperform. I understand more evaluations may be prohibitively expensive, but perhaps it would be worth it to find benchmark experimental results for some of these alternatives in the broader literature? ProFS could then be run on the same benchmark to get directly comparable results.

Clearly the linear projection method is powerful - if it does have a weakness, I imagine that it might be that it would be too heavy-handed/brittle in some sense if the subspaces end up being primarily about specific words. Are ProFS-aligned models still able to, for instance, have non-toxic discussions about words included in the toxic subspace? Or are they robust to being prompted to give toxic opinions using professional, nontoxic language? Furthermore, it is often desirable that models refuse to reply to harmful instructions (rather than reply in a nontoxic way). How well would the subspace approach work in aligning a model to refuse to reply?

comment.value:
Thank you for the insightful suggestions and questions! We hope our response helps address any concerns and look forward to your revised opinion and review.


**1.	Comparisons with more tuning-based alignment techniques:**


This is a very good point — our work seeks to bridge the gap between editing-based and tuning-based alignment approaches. To ground our analysis, we use DPO as a representative method for tuning-based alignment due to its widespread adoption. That said, we acknowledge the growing prevalence of alternative approaches and include a comparison with these methods in the discussion below.

In particular, we compare our method to KTO [1], which addresses the data bottleneck inherent in approaches like DPO and RLHF. While ProFS reduces the need for extensive labeled datasets, KTO eliminates the reliance on preference data altogether. Both methods, in their own ways, aim to mitigate the limitations posed by the data bottleneck. We use the experimental setup from [1], and run KTO on $2n$ datapoints, with other baselines using $n$ preference data pairs. We will also compare our method with IPO [2], which is a robust alternative to DPO with stronger theoretical guarantees. 

Table 1 below shows the sub-optimal performance of KTO in low data regimes. Notably, ProFS achieves significantly stronger performance; in Table 2, we also show similar trends with the Mistral 7B model.
 
**2.	Formatting issues:**

Thank you for the helpful suggestions! We have incorporated your suggestions regarding the readability of experimental results and citations.

**3.	Refusal to Toxic Prompts vs Non-Toxic Responses:**

This is an interesting insight, and we paraphrase the reviewer's concerns into the following:

1.	Too little deletion - Are only toxic words deleted, such that the model is capable of generating toxic opinions while simply avoiding toxic vocabulary?
2.	Too much deletion - Are entire toxic concepts deleted, such that the model is no longer able to hold non-toxic conversations about them?


For 1, we prompt the Mistral 7B model (ProFS aligned with HH-golden) with sequences that are free of toxic vocabulary but with toxic intent. Table 3 shows us that the model has a deeper understanding of toxic concepts, identifying the malicious intent of the prompts. Furthermore, without any explicit alignment towards refusal, the model defaults to this behavior on such prompts. 

To address 2, we prompt the model with sequences that contain toxic vocabulary but are free of toxic intent. Table 4 shows us that the model still has knowledge of these concepts, enabling instruction following capabilities over such concepts in non-toxic settings.

[1] KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization.

[2] A General Theoretical Paradigm to Understand Learning from Human Preferences.

[3] A mechanistic understanding of alignment algorithms: A case study on dpo and toxicity.

summary.value:
First, as wrote to the AC ( or at least I tried) I am not competent for reweing this manuscript and I hope that more qualifiedd reviewers will comment on the paper.

Nonetheless, I have read the paper, and I am trying to give useful feedback.

The paper introduces a novel alignment alternative called Project Filter for Subspaces (ProFS), which relies on running SVD on the model parameter space. The method tries to disentangle the so-called "toxic subspace." Overall, the paper is somewhat empirical yet tries to connect its approach with some theoretical work. From its experiment, the approach seems to work reasonably well.

I appreciate the presentation

For example, I can't tell if the equation
embedding  ≈ high-frequency vector + toxic vector + context-dependent vector
makes sense or it is wishful thinking. It seems that previous literature goes in this direction, but I myself am quite unsure about that.

strengths.value:
The paper read well and is easy to follow. I was able to follow it. The mathematical details for the use of SVD seem correct. From an outsider's perspective, the idea seems sensible.

The general idea is to look at the difference of the embedding matrix between label toxic and non toxic content, hence giving an idea of   what seems to differ between the two embeddings. The gist is to project the toxic embedding torward an not toxic embedding while keeping the non toxic embedding untouched.

The benchmarks seems quite extensive across multiple different model, and the robustness to misslabelling sounds like an interesting but my understanding is that is quite because this procedure keep the "distance" between the toxic vs non toxic embedding constant.

weaknesses.value: The problem that I have with this paper (and perhaps with this literature) is that the framework proposed matches really closely the literature, and so from a theoretical perspective, it sounds a bit like the authors assume some framework is designed for SVD to work and then suggest the using SVD in this context. While this is more of a theoretical criticism,    from a benchmark perspective, this approach seems to work decently. So perhaps I am a bit harsh.

questions.value:
Have you considered using other approaches like sparse SVD or Non-negative matrix factorization?
 Could you comment on the effect on the size of $T_l^0$ and its effect on reducing toxicity? 
I suspect that you need a decent amount of data. Have you tried testing a version with few rows (say just 100), and what is the recommended corpus size one should use?

comment.value:
Thank you for the insightful suggestions and questions! We hope our response helps address any concerns and look forward to your revised opinion and review.

**1. Use of SVD to Identify Concept Subspaces:**

The key geometric structure underlying this paper (and related literature) is the Linear representation hypothesis [1-6], which posits that various human-interpretable concepts are encoded in linear subspaces of model representations. This hypothesis has been considered mostly valid, as it is extensively validated empirically by a growing body of work on model editing. [8-14]

Our theoretical framework using the factor model has historical roots, as it is connected to classical literature outside language models, such as econometrics [15], where SVD is commonly used in many estimators. Our theoretical framework makes this connection clear compared with other modeling editing papers.

We think that our theoretical framework brings new insights to the alignment and model editing community: (i) identifying and analyzing the role of a large nonzero mean vector, which corresponds to the high-frequency stopwords; (ii) we offer a theoretical connection between DPO and our method in Appendix C, thus linking the structure of the weight space (where gradient updates lie) with the embedding space (where we make the structural assumption). We hope this addresses your concern!

**2. Alternatives to SVD:**

We would like to point out some key differences between SVD and alternative methods. 
- While Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is also based on a low-rank structure, NMF is commonly applied to count data due to its inherent non-negative constraints, which do not apply to hidden states. 
- Similarly, the sparsity structure is used to encourage the interpretability of each coordinate in the singular vectors (most usually in tabular data such as gene expression data). 

As far as we know, there is no observed sparsity structure or non-negativity structure in the hidden states from Transformers since the hidden states are real-valued vectors without any explicit constraint during the pre-training stage. Furthermore, ProFS is designed as a general-purpose method that operates without requiring such specific constraints. For this reason, we opt for standard SVD in our approach.

That being said, it would be very nice to exploit sparsity structure in much more complicated scenarios [16], and we will explore this in future work.

**3. Impact of $T_l^0$ size in reducing toxicity:**

ProFS is a highly sample-efficient approach – in Figure 2 (Section 7), we show that with as little as 50 datapoints (or rows of $T_l^0$), significant reductions in toxicity are achieved, with no significant detriment to perplexity. We also note this on tasks beyond toxicity: when aligned with the HH-Golden harmlessness dataset, the edited model achieves an 82% win rate over the original (Mistral 7B).

summary.value: The paper presents a novel flow matching method. This method can be applied to high dimensional data measured at non-equidistant time points without reducing dimensionality, so that the dynamics of the data are not oversimplified. The method is validated on several datasets and showed the improvement compared to existing methods.

strengths.value: This paper relied on the key observation/assumption that embedding vector $\approx$ high-frequency vector + toxic vector + context-dependent vector, and then used linear algebra tools including SVD to separate toxic vectors. I think an algorithm to separate toxic vectors based on the factorization of the embedding vector is original and nicely designed. Although, my research is not in LLM, so I cannot correctly evaluate originality or significance. I think the paper is in good quality and clearly written.

weaknesses.value:
As far as I understand, the weakness also comes from the key assumption that embedding vector $\approx$ high-frequency vector + toxic vector + context-dependent vector.

If toxic vector and other vectors are not linearly separable but have interaction terms, then we cannot really separate out toxic vectors by the projection matrix as Step 3 suggested. Could we guarantee that this interaction between the toxic and other features do not happen? Or can we verify that the interaction terms do not exist in the dataset? Designing a new algorithm considering the interaction terms would be beyond the scope of this paper, but this kind of discussion would be helpful to readers.

questions.value: As far as I understand, the algorithm is handling in fact a more flexible model than what is described in Equation (4). Currently in Equation (4), stopword parts of all data points are either one of two vectors, $a^{+}\mu$ for toxic data and $a^{-}\mu$ for non-toxic data. In Eqation (1) in Step 1, the linear space spanned by $\mu$ is removed from each data. Hence in Equation (4), it is not required that $x_{i}^{+}=a^{+}\mu$, i.e., stopword parts are all the same, but we can relax so that $x_{i}^{+}=a_{i}^{+}\mu$, we can let stopword parts be different but just on the linear space spanned by $\mu$. Also, we can relax so that $x_{i}^{-}=a_{i}^{-}\mu$. Is my understanding right, or is there some reason that stopword parts of all toxic data should be identical?

Thank you for the insightful suggestions and questions! We hope our response helps address any concerns and look forward to your revised opinion and review.

**1. Separability of Toxic and Non-Toxic Concepts:**

Our approach is based on the linear representation hypothesis [1-6], which posits that various human-interpretable concepts are encoded in linear subspaces of model representations. This hypothesis is supported theoretically by a latent variable modeling approach, and empirically supported by observations since word embeddings like Word2Vec [7], and more recently with successful editing approaches to make models more truthful [8-9], moral [9] and unbiased [10-14]. See [15] for a statistical framework from the statistics literature.

The interaction between toxicity and other “factors” seems to be weak as evidenced by the model editing literature as mentioned above. We also find toxicity is not entangled with other model capabilities. That being said, a more refined approach is perhaps using sparse autoencoder by Anthropic and OpenAI’s latest papers [16, 17], which will be our future exploration.

**2. Constraints on Stopwords:**

Your understanding is correct, and we thank you for bringing this up! We can indeed make our model our algorithm to a more flexible setting by defining $a_i$ per sequence, and have made the corresponding changes to Section 5 of our paper (we have uploaded the revised manuscript for reference).

display_title: Meta Review of Submission13296 by Area Chair 7EzR

metareview.value: This paper provides a tuning-free method called ProFS as an alternative to  direct preference optimization (DPO) to reduce model toxicity. Methods like DPO aim to make large language models (LLMs) safer by training them to mimic human preferences. However, these methods are complex, hard to control, and need a lot of data, and ProFS is more robust to noisy data and more efficient per sample. Reviewers find the contributions worthwhile though there are some strong assumptions on the embedding.

additional_comments_on_reviewer_discussi.value: Reviewers engaged in the rebuttal period and authors provided some clarification
